fields:
Give the molecular formula and charges of these polyatomic ions:
- Ammonium
- Hydroxide
- Nitrate
- Carbonate

- NH₄⁺
- OH⁻
- NO₃⁻
- CO₃²⁻

Give the molecular formula and charges of these polyatomic ions:
- Sulfate
- Hydrogencarbonate
- Phosphate

- SO₄²⁻
- HCO₃⁻
- PO₄³⁻
What is an orbital
A region of space with a high probability of containing an electron
Electron shell structure
Shell is divided into subshells which contain one or more orbitals
What is the Pauli exclusion principle
An orbital can contain a maximum of 2 electrons, which must have opposite spin states
What is the order in which orbitals are filled with electrons
In order of increasing energy with lower energy orbitals filled first: 1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d,4p
What is the order in which electrons are lost when forming cations
Electrons are removed from orbitals with the highest principle quantum number first
How many orbitals are in s and p subshells and what are their shapes

S - 1 spherical orbital
P - 3 dumbbell shaped orbitals

Give the molecular formula and charges of these polyatomic ions:
- perchlorate
- chlorate
- chlorite
- hypochlorite

- ClO₄⁻
- ClO₃⁻
- ClO₂⁻
- ClO⁻

Give the molecular formula and charges of these polyatomic ions:
- bromate 
- iodate 
- chromate
- acetate

- BrO₃⁻
- IO₃⁻
- CrO₄²⁻
- CH₃COO⁻

Give the molecular formula and charges of these polyatomic ions:
- cyanide 
- hydrogen phosphate
- dihydrogen phosphate

- CN⁻
- HPO₄²⁻
- H₂PO₄⁻
What is Hund's principle
Orbitals of the same energy are occupied singly with electrons of parallel spin before pairing occurs.
When are the 4s subshells not fully filled before the 3d subshells and why
For chromium and copper only, as 3d subshells are extra stable when they are half or fully filled so an electron is promoted from the 4s subshell to the 3d subshell
Which elements are classified into s, p, or d blocks and what does it mean

The block shows which subshell contains the highest energy electron
s block: Group 1-2
p block: Group 13-18
d block: Group 3-12
What is the number of orbitals in an s, p and d subshell

s - 1
p - 3
d - 5
How is shorthand notation written
[Previous noble gas] followed by the remaining electron configuration
How do the periods correlate to the subshell number

Period number = principle quantum number (s and p blocks)
Period number = principle quantum number +1 (d blocks)
Define ionisation energy
The energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms or ions of an element
Describe and explain the general trend in the magnitude of successive ionisation energies (2)

- Increases
- Removing the next electron away from an increasing positive charge ion
Explain how successive ionisation energies provide evidence for electron shells (3)

- The sharp jump in the energy required to remove an electron
- indicates the electrostatic force of attraction between the valence electron and the nucleus has dramatically increased 
- due to the electrons being in a shell closer to the nucleus
3 factors that affect ionisation energy

- Distance between the nucleus and the outermost shell
- Nuclear charge
- Electron shielding
Trend in 1st ionisation energy of each element across a period (6)

- there is a general increase across a period
- the valence electron across a period is being removed from the same energy level
- similar electron shielding between the nucleus and the outermost shell
- nuclear charge is increasing 
- small decrease in atomic radius
- therefore a stronger electrostatic attraction between the outermost electron and nucleus
Trend in 1st ionisation energy of each element down a group (6)

- there is a decrease in ionisation energy down a group
- valence electron is being removed from a higher energy level
- the valence electron is at an increased distance from the nucleus
- the electron shielding between the valence electron and the nucleus has increased
- the increase in atomic radius and electron shielding outweighs the increase in nuclear charge
- decrease in the electrostatic attraction between the valence electron and the nucleus
When does the trend in ionisation energy across a period deviate

- Beryllium -> Boron and Magnesium -> Aluminium
- Nitrogen -> Oxygen and Phosphorus -> Sulfur
Explain the drop in IE from Be to B (2)

- The valence electron in B is being removed from a 2p subshell as opposed to a 2s subshell
- The 2s subshell shields the 2p subshell
Explain the drop in IE from N to O (2)

- Because in O spin pairing has occurred for the first time in the 3p subshell
- resulting in an increase in repulsion between electrons so the electron is lost more easily
State how the relative abundance of two isotopes can be found [2]

- compare the number of particles of each isotope detected
- in a mass spectrometer
What are the 5 stages of mass spectrometry

- Vaporisation
- Ionisation
- Acceleration
- Deflection
- Detection
What happens during the ionisation stage of mass spectrometry
The sample is bombarded with high energy electrons that knock one or more electrons off of each atom/molecule to form positive ions
What happens during the acceleration stage of mass spectrometry

A potential difference between two oppositely charged plates creates an electric field that accelerates the positive ions towards and through an opening in the negatively charged plate, giving them approximately the same kinetic energy.
What happens during the deflection stage of mass spectrometry

A magnetic field created by magnets around the path of the ions exerts a force perpendicular to their direction of travel. Ions with a lower mass to charge ratio are deflected more, as lower mass ions are easier to change in direction, while ions with a higher charge experience a greater force from the magnetic field.
What happens during the detection stage of mass spectrometry

Ions with the same mass to charge ratio follow the same path and are detected together electrically, with the size of the electric signal giving their relative abundance. A mass spectrum is produced, plotting relative abundance against mass to charge ratio.
Define relative atomic mass
The weighted average mass of an atom of an element relative to 1/12th of the mass of an atom of the isotope carbon-12
Define relative isotopic mass
The mass of one atom of an isotope relative to 1/12th of the mass of an atom of the isotope carbon-12
Define periodicity and give 3 examples
A repeating pattern in a property across a period (ionisation energy, atomic radius, boiling point)
Define atomic/ionic radius
The distance between the nucleus and outermost electron shell
Define isoelectronic ions
Ions of different elements with the same electron configuration
Describe and explain the trend in atomic radius across a period [4]

- Decreases
- There is an increase in nuclear charge
- There is similar electron shielding between the nucleus and outermost shell
- Electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and valence electron increases
Describe an explain the trend in atomic radius down a group [5]

- Increases
- There is an additional electron shell
- so electron shielding between the nucleus and outermost shell increases
- This outweighs the increased nuclear charge
- so electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and valence electron decreases
Describe and explain trend in ionic radius for isoelectronic ions [4]

- Decreases
- There is an increase in nuclear charge
- Electron shielding between the nucleus and outermost shell is the same
- Electrostatic attraction between nucleus and valence electron increases
What are the 3 stages of flame emission spectroscopy

1. A sample of metal ions is placed into the flame
2. The electromagnetic radiation emitted by the sample is passed into a spectroscope
3. The spectroscope separates the electromagnetic radiation into its different wavelengths, producing a line spectrum
Describe what happens in terms of electrons during flame emission spectroscopy

Thermal energy from the flame is transferred to the electrons, exciting them and causing them to move to higher energy levels. The electrons then move to lower energy levels, releasing energy as photons of electromagnetic radiation.
How do atom emissions spectra provide evidence for the existence of quantum shells/energy levels

When electrons move to lower energy levels, the electromagnetic radiation is emitted at specific discrete frequencies, producing a line spectrum rather than a continuous spectrum. This shows that only specific energy differences are possible, providing evidence that electrons must reside in discrete energy levels.
How to read an atom emission spectrum

Each line corresponds to electromagnetic radiation emitted when an electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level. 
A smaller wavelength of radiation corresponds to a higher energy photon and the energy of the photon corresponds to the difference in energy between the two energy levels.
Explain the trend in melting point across a period in metallic elements

- Increases
- There is a decrease in ionic radius of the metal ion (due to an increase in nuclear charge and electron shielding being the same)
- There are a greater number of delocalised electrons 
- The ion has a higher positive charge
- Greater electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
- More energy required to overcome the metallic bonding
Explain why Silicon has such a high melting point compared to the rest of period 3

- It is a giant covalent structure
- with many strong covalent bonds
- which need a lot of energy to be broken

* A student suggested that the difference in the rates of reaction of strontium and barium
with water is due to the difference in the sum of their first and second ionisation energies.
Discuss this suggestion. [6]

- The sum of the first two ionisation energies for barium is lower
- since barium has more shells of electrons and a larger atomic radius
- and more shielding
- These outweigh 
- barium having a greater nuclear charge
- so barium loses its outer electrons more easily and reacts faster
2 requirements for an element to be a transition metal

- Must be a d-block element
- Must form at least one stable ion with an incomplete d-subshell
When is relative formula mass used and when is relative molecular mass used

Formula mass: Giant structures
Molecular mass: Simple molecular structures
What are the 5 types of structures and the particles involved in them

Monoatomic: Atoms
Simple molecular: Molecules
Giant covalent: Atoms
Giant ionic: Ions 
Giant metallic: Ions and delocalised electrons
Which substances are monoatomic
Group 0
Which substances are simple molecular
Most non-metal elements and compounds apart from group 0
Which 4 substances are giant covalent
Diamond, graphite, silicon, silicon dioxide
Which substances are giant ionic
Most compounds made from metals and non-metals combined
Why are metals soft (3)

- The atoms/ion are the same size
- so they are arranged in regular layers
- which can slide over each other easily
Why are alloys hard (3)

- The atoms/ions are different sizes
- so they are arranged in irregular layers
- which can not slide over each other easily
Why do metals have a high melting point (3)

- Metals have a giant lattice structure 
- with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the positive metal ions and negative delocalised valence electrons
- which require lots of energy to overcome
Why do metals conduct electricity

- Metals have delocalised valence electrons from the cations
- which are free to move around
- and carry charge throughout the structure
Why does Cl2 have a low melting point (3)

- It is a simple molecular structure
- with weak intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules
- which can be overcome with little energy
Why does diamond have a high melting point (4)

- Diamond is a giant covalent structure
- where each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms
- There are many strong covalent bonds
- which need lots of energy to be broken
Why is diamond hard (3)

- Diamond is a giant covalent structure
- where each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms
- creating a rigid lattice where atoms cannot slide past each other
Why does NaCl have a high melting point (3)

- NaCl is a giant ionic lattice structure
- made up of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions 
- which require lots of energy to be overcome
Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity as a solid but not a liquid
As a solid the ions are fixed in position in the giant ionic lattice but as a liquid the ions are free to move around and carry charge.
What is a dative covalent bond (co-ordinate bond)
When both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom
What is a lone pair of electrons
A pair of electrons that are not involved in a covalent bond
2 criteria for a dative covalent bond to form

- There must be a lone pair on one of the atoms in the bonded pair
- There must be a vacant orbital on the other atom in the bonded pair
4 examples of dative covalent bonds

- Carbon monoxide 
- Ammonium
- Ammonia with boron trifluoride 
- 2AlCl3
Define electron deficient species and name 3 examples

Species that do not have complete octets
- Aluminium
- Boron
- Beryllium
What are expanded octets
When elements in period 3 and higher have more than 8 electrons in their valence shell
Exam Q: Explain the shape of this molecule [4]

- There are _ bonding pairs and _ lone pairs
- Electron pairs repel and try to position themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion
- There are no lone pairs so electron pairs repel equally 
  or lone pair - bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair - bonding pair repulsion
- Has a _ shape with a bond angle of  _
Shape and bond angle when there are 2 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs

Linear 
180 degrees
Shape and bond angle when there are 3 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs

Trigonal planar
120 degrees
Shape and bond angle when there are 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs

Tetrahedral
109.5 degrees
Shape and bond angle when there are 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair

Pyramidal
107 degrees
Shape and bond angle when there are 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs

Bent
104.5 degrees
Shape and bond angle when there are 5 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs

Trigonal bipyramidal 
90 and 120 degrees
Shape and bond angle when there are 6 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs

Octahedral 
90 degrees
Define electronegativity
The ability of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond
Factors affecting electronegativity

- Nuclear charge
- Atomic radius
- Electron shielding
Describe and explain the trend in electronegativity across a period [5]

- Increases
- Increase in nuclear charge
- Electron shielding is similar
- Atomic radius decreases slightly
- Greater electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and shared pair of electrons
Describe and explain the trend in electronegativity down a group [5]

- Decreases
- More shells so atomic radius increases
- Increase in electron shielding
- These outweigh the increase in nuclear charge
- Weaker electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and shared pair of electrons
4 most electronegative elements in decreasing order
Fluorine, Oxygen, Nitrogen, Chlorine
Define a non polar covalent bond
One in which there is an equal sharing of electrons between atoms that are bonded together due to there being little to no difference in electronegativity between the atoms bonded
Define a polar covalent bond
One in which there is an unequal sharing of electrons between atoms that are bonded together due to there being a large enough difference in electronegativity between the atoms bonded
Explain how electronegativity difference correlates to the type of bond

0.0-0.5: Still effectively evenly shared so non polar covalent 
0.5-1.7: Significantly closer to the more electronegative atom, giving both atoms partial charges, so polar covalent
1.7+: Counts as a full transfer of electrons, giving both atoms full charges, so ionic
Define a dipole
A representation of the separation of charge pointing from δ+ to δ-
Define a polar molecule
A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge across the whole molecule and has at least one permanent dipole
Explain why this molecule is polar [2]

- Bond dipoles cancel out
- due to a symmetric _ shape
Explain why this shape is non-polar [2]

- Bond dipoles do not cancel out
- due to an asymmetric _ shape
Name 3 molecule shapes that are symmetrical

- Linear
- Trigonal planar
- Tetrahedral (only when all the bonds are the same)
Name 3 molecule shapes that are always asymmetrical

- Bent
- Pyramidal
- Tetrahedral (when the bonds are not the same)
Sign for partial charges
Lower case del, δ+ and δ-

Formulae, Equations and Amounts of Substance

fields: What is an empirical formula
The simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound
What is a molecular formula
The actual number of each type of atom in a molecule
What is percentage yield
Actual yield as a percentage of the theoretical yield (use mol or mass)
What is atom economy
The percentage of reactant atoms that end up as useful products (use mr)
What is a limitation of percentage yield
It does not account for the amount of by-products produced
What is green chemistry
The sustainable design of chemical products and processes to minimise environmental impact and waste
3 principles of green chemistry

- Prevent waste
- Improve atom economy of chemical processes
- Using less hazardous substances
3 things that lead to %age yield being less than 100%

- Reaction is incomplete
- Side reactions occur
- Product is lost during separation/purification
Who were the three scientists that contributed to the ideal gas equation and what did they investigate

Boyle: P ∝ 1/V, T and n constant

Charles: V ∝ T, P and n constant

Avogadro: V ∝ n, P and T constant
State the ideal gas equation

PV=nRT

P in Pa
V in m^3
n in moles
T in Kelvin
What is the value and unit of the ideal constant
R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
Equivalence point vs end point

The equivalence point is the theoretical point at which the amount of one reactant has been added to completely react with the other reactant, whereas the end point is the observed point at which the indicator changes colour, which should be close to the equivalence point.
Define a standard solution
A solution with an accurately known concentration
Define a primary standard
A chemical that can be weighed out accurately to make up a standard solution
3 criteria for a primary standard

- very pure
- doesn't gain or lose mass when in air
- has a relatively high molar mass so that weighing errors have less effect
Formula for quantitative distillation of a chemical
Conc added x vol added = solution conc x solution vol
How to prepare a standard solution from a primary standard (CP2) [6]

- Transfer entire known sample to beaker
- dissolve in deionised water by stirring with rod
- transfer via filter funnel into volumetric flask
- rinse beaker, rod and funnel washings with distilled water into flask for quantitative transfer
- add distilled water with a pipette dropwise till the bottom of meniscus at eye level is on the mark
- add stopper and invert repeatedly to mix contents thoroughly
Colour change of methyl orange for a low to high ph
Red to yellow
Colour change for methyl red from low to high ph
Red to yellow
Colour change of bromothymol blue from low to high ph
Yellow to blue
Colour change of phenolpthalein from low to high ph
Colourless to pink
5 compounds that are always soluble

Group 1 salts
Ammonium salts
Nitrates
First 3 halides (chloride, bromide, iodide) apart from silver and lead
Sulfates apart from lead and barium
2 compounds that are always insoluble

Carbonates apart from group 1 and ammonium
Hydroxides apart from group 1 and lower down group 2
Define molar volume of a gas
The volume occupied by one mole of a gas at a specified temperature and pressure
How to carry out a titration (CP3) [6]

- Measure 50cm3 of sulfuric acid in a beaker and fill burette with the solution using a funnel 
- Measure 25cm3 of standard sodium carbonate solution using a pipette and add to a conical flask that has been rinsed with distilled water
- Add 2-3 drops of methyl orange and place the flask on a white tile beneath the burette
- Read the position of the meniscus in the burette and record the initial reading to the nearest 0.05cm3
- Add the acid to the carbonate dropwise until the indicator turns salmon-pink
- Record the final burette reading and calculate the volume of acid used
- Repeat until at least two concordant results are obtained
How to find the volume of one mole of hydrogen gas (CP1) [6]

1. Clean a small strip of magnesium to remove any oxide layer.

  2. Accurately measure and record the mass of the magnesium using a balance (mass should be no greater than 0.050 g).

  3. Add 25.0 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid to a conical flask.

  4. Add the magnesium to the acid and immediately seal the flask with a bung connected to a gas syringe.

  5. Collect the hydrogen gas produced in the gas syringe until all the magnesium has reacted. The hydrochloric acid is in excess to ensure the magnesium is the limiting reactant.

  6. Record the volume of hydrogen gas produced.
Define a hydrocarbon
A compound of hydrogen and carbon only
What are the 5 types of formulae and what do they show

Empirical - simplest whole number ratio of atoms of elements in a compound
Molecular - number of atoms of each element in a molecule of a compound
Structural - shows how atoms are arranged in a molecule of a compound
Displayed - shows all the atoms and covalent bonds present in a molecule of a compound
Skeletal - represents a C-C bond as one line and only functional groups are written out
List the functional groups from highest priority to lowest with their suffixes/prefixes

- Carboxylic acid (-COOH): -oic acid
- Ester (-COO-): -oate
- Aldehyde (-CHO): -al
- Ketone (C=O): -one
- Alcohol (-OH): -ol
- Amine (-NH2): -amine
- Alkene (C=C): -ene
- Alkane (C-C): -ane
- Halogen: fluoro-
- Alkyl (CH3): methyl-
What are the three hydrocarbon homologous series

Alkane (CnH2n+2)
Alkene (CnH2n)
Cycloalkane (CnH2n)
Define a functional group
A small group of atoms or a single halogen atom that gives a compound its characteristic chemical properties and reactions
Define a homologous series
A series of organic compounds that have the same functional group, with each successive member differing by CH2
How to name organic compounds

1. Find the stem which is based on the longest continuous carbon chain
2. Find the suffix which shows the highest priority functional group
3. Find the prefix which shows the type and number groups of lower priority than the homologous hydrocarbon series
4. Use numbers to show the position of the groups, choosing the direction that gives the highest priority functional group the lowest number, and the lowest possible set of numbers for the remaining groups
What are the 7 types of organic reactions

Addition
Elimination
Substitution
Oxidation
Reduction
Hydrolysis
Polymerisation
What happens in an addition reaction
Joining 2 or more unsaturated molecules to produce a saturated molecule
What happens in an elimination reaction
A molecule is lost from a saturated molecule to form an unsaturated molecule
What happens in a substitution reaction
An atom/group replaces another atom/group
What happens in oxidation and reduction reactions

Oxidation: a species loses electrons
Reduction: a species gains electrons
What happens in a hydrolysis reaction
Bonds break due to a reaction involving water
What happens in a polymerisation reaction
Lots of simple molecules are joined together to form a giant molecule
Define a species
An atom, ion, radical or molecule
How and why does boiling point change as hydrocarbons get longer
Longer chains have a higher boiling point due to there being more electrons which means stronger Van der Waal's forces between molecules, which needs more energy to be overcome
Define a free radical
A species containing an unpaired electron (only one electron in the orbital)
2 types of fission

Homolytic: both atoms take one electron from the bonded pair forming two radicals
Heterolytic: one atom takes both electrons from the bonded pair forming a cation and an anion which gains a lone pair
Define a nucleophile
A species that donates a lone pair of electrons to another species
Reaction vs mechanism

A reaction is an equation showing the reactants and products whilst a mechanism shows how a reaction occurs step by step, using curly arrows to show the movement of electrons. Different mechanisms can result in the same reaction.
Name the 3 stages of free radical substitution

- Initiation
- Propagation
- Termination
Describe the initiation stage of free radical substitution
Sunlight or UV rays provide energy for homolytic fission to break a covalent bond, producing two free radicals
Describe the propagation stage of free radical substitution

A free radical produced by initiation reacts with a non-radical molecule, taking an atom from it to make itself non radical and turning the molecule into a new free radical. This new free radical reacts with more non-radical molecules in a chain reaction until termination.
Describe the termination stage of free radical substitution
Two free radicals react together forming a covalent bond and producing a non-radical molecule
How are free radicals formed
Through homolytic fission, where a covalent bond breaks and each atom takes one electron from the bonding pair, resulting in two species containing an unpaired electron, forming two free radicals
